title: In the Beginning Was the Word
subtitle: John 1:1–18
description: Before the manger and the genealogy, John's Gospel opens in eternity, with the Word who was with God and was God.
paragraphs: The fourth Gospel does not begin with a manger, a genealogy, or an angel in a small town. It begins before all of those, in the very words Genesis starts with, and it asks the reader to look at Jesus from that height first. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Before anything was made, the Word already was, with God and himself God. “Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made.” What was in him, John says, was life itself, and that life was the light of the whole human race: “In Him was life, and that life was the light of men.” The light is already shining into a darkness that pushes against it, and the prologue gives away the end of that contest in its fifth sentence: “The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.”

Before the Word steps into the story, a witness steps out to point at him. “There came a man who was sent from God. His name was John.” The Baptist enters this Gospel the way the prologue insists he be understood, as a witness and nothing more. “He himself was not the Light, but he came to testify about the Light.” His whole errand was to stand beside the light and say where it was, so that through him everyone might believe. And the one he pointed to was already on his way: “The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.”

What happened when he arrived is the sorrow at the center of the prologue, stated as flatly as the glory. “He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him.” The maker stood in his own world and was not known. It cut deeper at home: “He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him.” But the sentence does not end there, because this Gospel turns on the ones who did receive him. To them he gave a right: “But to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God”. And the birth that follows is no human doing: “children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God.”

Then the prologue lands on the claim the whole Gospel rests on. “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us.” The eternal Word of the first verse has a body now, and an address among human beings. And John writes as one of the people who were there, in the plural: “We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.” Glory, in this Gospel, is not a theory about God. It is something witnesses saw, in a man full of grace and truth.

The witness speaks once more before the prologue closes: “This is He of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.’” The cry explains the Baptist's whole place in the story: the one who came after him in the ministry was before him in existence. What the witnesses received out of that fullness is summed up in one doubled phrase: “From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace.” Then, in the seventeenth verse of his Gospel, John finally says the name the whole prologue has been circling: “For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” And the last line looks back up to where the first line began. “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.” The unseen God has been made known, not by a voice from a cloud or a tablet of stone, but by the Son at his side, who became flesh and lived among us. The story can begin.

title: The Lamb of God
subtitle: John 1:19–34
description: A priestly delegation interrogates John the Baptist, and the next day he points at Jesus and gives him his first public title.
paragraphs: The first people to come asking questions in this Gospel are not seekers. They are investigators, sent from Jerusalem to the Jordan to find out who John the Baptist claimed to be. “Who are you?” they asked him, and John would not leave them guessing. “I am not the Christ.” They worked down their list of hopes. Was he Elijah, come back as Malachi promised? “I am not.” Was he the Prophet Moses spoke of? “No.” The delegation needed something to carry back to the men who sent them, so they pressed him one more time: “Who are you? We need an answer for those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”

John answered with somebody else's words, the prophet Isaiah's: “I am a voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Make straight the way for the Lord.’” That was his whole self-description, a voice, not a destination. The Pharisees in the party had a sharper question. If he was none of the expected figures, by what right was he baptizing? “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?”

His answer pointed past himself again. “I baptize with water,” John replied, “but among you stands One you do not know. He is the One who comes after me, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.” All of it happened, John is careful to say, at Bethany beyond the Jordan, where the baptizing was going on. The unknown man was already standing in the crowd, and the witness's work was nearly done.

The next day it happened. “The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” It is the first title this Gospel gives Jesus in public, and it is a title about dying, a lamb for the sin of the whole world, not Israel only. John tied it to the prologue's strange arithmetic: “This is He of whom I said, ‘A man who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.’” Then he admitted something easy to miss. “I myself did not know Him, but the reason I came baptizing with water was that He might be revealed to Israel.” His own water ministry had one purpose, to bring this man into the open.

So John told them how he knew. “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Him.” He had been given the sign in advance by the One who sent him to baptize: “The man on whom you see the Spirit descend and rest is He who will baptize with the Holy Spirit.” Water was John's element; the Spirit would be this man's. And the witness closed his testimony with the verdict the whole Gospel will spend twenty chapters proving: “I have seen and testified that this is the Son of God.”

title: Come and See
subtitle: John 1:35–51
description: The first disciples come to Jesus one by one, each brought by somebody else, and Nathanael is undone by a fig tree.
paragraphs: The next day John was standing with two of his own disciples when Jesus walked by, and the witness did his work one more time: “Look, the Lamb of God!” The two men heard it and, on the strength of their teacher's pointing, followed Jesus down the road. Jesus turned and asked them the first question he asks anyone in this Gospel: “What do you want?” They answered with a question of their own. “Rabbi” (which means Teacher), “where are You staying?” His answer becomes the invitation the whole Gospel keeps repeating: “Come and see.” They went, they saw where he was staying, and they spent that day with him. John notes the hour almost in passing, about the tenth hour, the way a man remembers the hour something began.

One of the two was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, and the first thing the first follower did was go and find somebody. “He first found his brother Simon and told him, “We have found the Messiah” (which is translated as Christ). Andrew brought his brother to Jesus, the first in a chain of people in this chapter who bring people. Jesus looked at the new arrival and renamed him on the spot: “You are Simon son of John. You will be called Cephas” (which is translated as Peter). Before Simon has said a word in this Gospel, he has a new name and a future built into it.

The next day Jesus set out for Galilee and found Philip, and gave him the shortest of calls, to follow him. Philip was from Bethsaida, the same fishing town as Andrew and Peter, and he did what Andrew had done. He found Nathanael and announced, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law, the One the prophets foretold”, then named him: “Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.” Nathanael's answer is the most honest skepticism in the chapter: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Philip did not argue. He borrowed the invitation Jesus had used the day before: “Come and see,” said Philip.

What Nathanael walked into was not an argument but a man who already knew him. “When Jesus saw Nathanael approaching, He said of him, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” Startled, Nathanael asked how he knew him, and Jesus answered with a picture nobody else could have seen: “Before Philip called you, I saw you under the fig tree.” It undid him completely. “Rabbi,” Nathanael answered, “You are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!” Jesus received the confession and gently measured it. “Do you believe just because I told you I saw you under the fig tree? You will see greater things than these.” Then he opened the promise out to all of them, to a stairway older than Jacob's ladder, with himself in the place of the ladder: “Truly, truly, I tell you, you will all see heaven open and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”

title: Water into Wine
subtitle: John 2:1–12
description: At a wedding in Cana the wine runs out, and Jesus turns six jars of wash water into the finest wine of the feast.
paragraphs: On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and Jesus' mother was there, and Jesus and his disciples had been invited too. It was an ordinary village celebration, and it was sliding toward a small social disaster that everyone in that culture would feel. When the wine ran out, Jesus' mother said to him, “They have no more wine.” She did not ask for anything outright. She just laid the fact in front of her son and left it there.

His answer draws a line she seems to accept at once. “Woman, what is that to you and to Me?” Jesus replied. “My hour has not yet come.” It is the first sounding of this Gospel's deepest refrain, the hour that hangs over everything he does and has not yet arrived. His mother did not argue with it. She turned to the servants and gave them the only instruction that matters in the story: “Do whatever He tells you.”

Standing nearby were six stone water jars, set there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty to thirty gallons. Jesus told the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” So they filled them to the brim, all six, well over a hundred gallons of well water hauled and poured for no reason anyone could see. Then he gave the strange order: “Now draw some out,” He said, “and take it to the master of the banquet.” They did so, carrying a cup of what they had drawn as water to the man in charge of the feast.

The master of the banquet tasted it, and the water had been turned into wine, and he did not know where it had come from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew. He called the bridegroom aside, astonished at the order of the serving: “Everyone serves the fine wine first, and then the cheap wine after the guests are drunk. But you have saved the fine wine until now!” The bridegroom got credit for a generosity he had not performed, the servants knew more than the master of the feast, and the one who did it stayed in the background of his own first sign.

John will not let the moment pass as a wedding anecdote. “Jesus performed this, the first of His signs, at Cana in Galilee.” First of his signs, he calls it, a sign pointing somewhere, and then he says what it did: “He thus revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him.” The men who had followed him for a week on a witness's word now believed on the evidence of their own eyes. After the wedding, Jesus went down to Capernaum with his mother and brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there a few days, a family and a new company together before the road turned toward Jerusalem.

title: Zeal for His Father's House
subtitle: John 2:13–25
description: At his first Passover Jesus clears the temple courts with a whip and answers the demand for a sign with a riddle about three days.
paragraphs: When the Jewish Passover was near, Jesus went up to Jerusalem, and a reader who knows the other Gospels has to stop here. In Matthew, Mark, and Luke, what happens next waits until the last week of his life. John puts it at the front, and John means it to be at the front. In the temple courts Jesus found the Passover business in full operation: “men selling cattle, sheep, and doves, and money changers seated at their tables.” Pilgrims needed animals for sacrifice and temple currency for the tax, and the courts of God's house had become the place where both were sold.

What he did was not a gesture. “So He made a whip out of cords and drove all from the temple courts, both sheep and cattle. He poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables.” He made the whip himself, which means he looked at the scene, decided, and took the time. To the dove sellers, whose cages could not be tipped, he spoke: “Get these out of here! How dare you turn My Father’s house into a marketplace!” My Father's house. The boy who once told his parents he had to be in his Father's house was now a man clearing it with a whip.

His disciples, watching, remembered a line from the Psalms and stored it away as the explanation: “Zeal for Your house will consume Me.” The authorities had a more immediate response. A man who disrupts the temple trade at Passover, with Roman soldiers watching from the fortress next door, has to answer for his authority: “What sign can You show us to prove Your authority to do these things?”

His answer was a riddle nobody in the courtyard could solve: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up again.” The Jews heard stone and scaffolding. “This temple took forty-six years to build,” the Jews replied, “and You are going to raise it up in three days?” Herod's great rebuilding project, decades in the making, raised in three days. It sounded like madness, and John steps out of the scene to tell the reader plainly what the courtyard could not know: “But Jesus was speaking about the temple of His body.” Only after the resurrection did the disciples put the two halves together: “Then they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.”

Meanwhile the feast went on, and Jerusalem began its long, divided argument about him. “While He was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many people saw the signs He was doing and believed in His name.” It is the belief John has been celebrating since Cana, and here he puts a shadow across it. “But Jesus did not entrust Himself to them, for He knew them all.” The crowds believed in him; he did not yet believe in them, and John gives the reason in one of the Gospel's coldest lines: “He did not need any testimony about man, for He knew what was in a man.” The first Passover of the ministry ends with a city impressed, a temple challenged, and a man who knew exactly what human enthusiasm was worth.

title: You Must Be Born Again
subtitle: John 3:1–21
description: Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews, comes to Jesus at night and hears that seeing the kingdom requires a second birth.
paragraphs: The Jerusalem belief that Jesus would not trust produced one honest man who came in the dark. “Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a leader of the Jews. He came to Jesus at night.” He was not a seeker off the street. He was a member of the ruling council, a teacher of Israel, and he came with a conclusion his colleagues had reached from the Passover signs: “Rabbi, we know that You are a teacher who has come from God. For no one could perform the signs You are doing if God were not with him.” It was a respectful opening, and Jesus ignored it completely and answered a question Nicodemus had not asked.

“Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again.” The answer landed on the old scholar like a riddle in the wrong language. “How can a man be born when he is old?” Nicodemus asked. “Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time to be born?” Jesus did not soften it. “Truly, truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God unless he is born of water and the Spirit. Flesh is born of flesh, but spirit is born of the Spirit.” Birth is not in the child's control the first time, and it is not in the seeker's control the second. “Do not be amazed that I said, ‘You must be born again.’ The wind blows where it wishes. You hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it is going. So it is with everyone born of the Spirit.”

Nicodemus could only repeat himself: “How can this be?” And now Jesus pressed the teacher of Israel on his own ground. “You are Israel’s teacher,” said Jesus, “and you do not understand these things? Truly, truly, I tell you, we speak of what we know, and we testify to what we have seen, and yet you people do not accept our testimony.” Earthly things had baffled him; what about heavenly things? Only one man could report on those: “No one has ascended into heaven except the One who descended from heaven”. The Son of Man had come down, and the way back ran through a lifting up that Nicodemus knew from his own Scriptures, the bronze snake Moses raised in the wilderness: “Just as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in Him may have eternal life.”

Then the talk opens into the sentence the whole world knows. “For God so loved the world that He gave His one and only Son, that everyone who believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life.” The giving, not the condemning, is the errand: “For God did not send His Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through Him.” And the judgment, when it comes, is a verdict people pass on themselves by their response to the gift: “Whoever believes in Him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe has already been condemned, because he has not believed in the name of God’s one and only Son.” Whether the evangelist is still reporting Jesus' words here or has begun speaking in his own voice, the Gospel never marks the seam, and the talk runs on in the same light-and-darkness language the prologue used.

“And this is the verdict: The Light has come into the world, but men loved the darkness rather than the Light because their deeds were evil.” The darkness is not ignorance in this Gospel. It is preference, a love of cover: “Everyone who does evil hates the Light, and does not come into the Light for fear that his deeds will be exposed. But whoever practices the truth comes into the Light, so that it may be seen clearly that what he has done has been accomplished in God.” Nicodemus came at night, and John leaves him in the conversation without recording his answer. He will appear twice more in this Gospel, and each time a little further out of the dark.

title: He Must Increase
subtitle: John 3:22–36
description: John the Baptist answers his disciples' jealousy with the joy of the bridegroom's friend: he must increase, I must decrease.
paragraphs: After the night conversation, Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and the ministry the Baptist had announced began running alongside the Baptist's own. Jesus baptized there, through his disciples, and John was baptizing too, at Aenon near Salim, because the water was plentiful there. John adds a parenthesis the other Gospels never give at this point in the story: “(For John had not yet been thrown into prison.)” Both baptisms, both crowds, one countryside, and it could not last without somebody counting.

The counting started with an argument about ceremonial washing between John's disciples and a certain Jew, and it ended at John's feet as a complaint about Jesus: “Look, Rabbi, the One who was with you beyond the Jordan, the One you testified about”. Then the alarm itself: “He is baptizing, and everyone is going to Him.” Everyone is going to him. It was meant to sting, the loyal staff warning the leader that his crowds were draining away to his own discovery.

John's answer is the most contented speech in the Gospel. “A man can receive only what is given him from heaven.” His ministry was a gift with edges, and he knew where the edges were. “You yourselves can testify that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but am sent ahead of Him.’” Then he reached for the picture of a wedding, the same celebration where this Gospel's first sign had happened. “The bride belongs to the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom stands and listens for him, and is overjoyed to hear the bridegroom’s voice. That joy is mine, and it is now complete.” The friend of the bridegroom does not compete with the bridegroom. Hearing his voice is the job, and the joy.

Then he said it in nine words that have outlived every ministry since: “He must increase; I must decrease.” No bargaining in it, no sadness either. The voice of the prologue had pointed, the crowds had gone, and the witness counted the loss as completion.

The chapter closes with a testimony that rises above both men, whether it is John's voice still speaking or the evangelist's own, for the Gospel leaves that seam unmarked here as well. “The One who comes from above is above all.” The Son testifies to what he has seen and heard in heaven, and the tragedy of the age is the shrug that greets him: “He testifies to what He has seen and heard, yet no one accepts His testimony.” To accept it is to sign one's name to a verdict about God himself: “Whoever accepts His testimony has certified that God is truthful. For the One whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for God gives the Spirit without limit. The Father loves the Son and has placed all things in His hands.” And the last word of the chapter is a fork in the road with no third path: “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Whoever rejects the Son will not see life. Instead, the wrath of God remains on him.”

title: The Woman at the Well
subtitle: John 4:1–26
description: At Jacob's well at noon, Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink and tells her about living water and true worship.
paragraphs: Jesus left Judea because the Pharisees were starting to count his baptisms against John's, and the road back to Galilee ran through Samaria, the country respectable Jews walked around. John says he had to pass through it. “So He came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the plot of ground that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.” Jacob's well was there, and Jesus, weary from the journey, sat down by it at about the sixth hour, noon, in the heat. His disciples had gone into town to buy food. A Samaritan woman came to draw water, alone at an hour when women did not usually come alone, and the tired Jew asked her a question that crossed every line on the map: “Give Me a drink.”

Her surprise is the first thing in the conversation. “You are a Jew,” said the woman. “How can You ask for a drink from me, a Samaritan woman?” John pauses to explain for readers who need it: Jews do not associate with Samaritans. Jesus did not defend the request. He redirected it entirely: “If you knew the gift of God and who is asking you for a drink, you would have asked Him, and He would have given you living water.” A gift, a giver, and water that is somehow alive. She heard it in the only register she had, the practical one.

“Sir,” the woman replied, “You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep. Where then will You get this living water? Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock?” It was a fair taunt. He had no bucket, and the well under their feet had a pedigree a thousand years long. Jesus answered her in her own terms and then lifted the terms: “Everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again. But whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst. Indeed, the water I give him will become in him a fount of water springing up to eternal life.” Jacob's well had to be visited daily for centuries. This water would become a spring inside the drinker.

She asked for it on the practical level still, and who can blame her: “Sir, give me this water so that I will not get thirsty and have to keep coming here to draw water.” No more daily trips in the noon heat, no more jar. Jesus answered her request with an instruction that walked straight into the hidden part of her life: “Go, call your husband and come back.” “I have no husband,” the woman replied. It was the truest and least true sentence she could have chosen. “You are correct to say that you have no husband. In fact, you have had five husbands, and the man you now have is not your husband. You have spoken truthfully.” The stranger at the well knew her whole history, and the conversation changed temperature.

“I see that You are a prophet,” she said, and reached for the great standing argument between her people and his: “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.” Jesus did not settle the argument. He announced its end. “Believe Me, woman,” Jesus replied, “a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” Geography was about to stop being the question: “But a time is coming and has now come when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth, for the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him. God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth.” She took refuge in the future, where her people kept their hopes: “I know that Messiah” (called Christ) “is coming. When He comes, He will explain everything to us.” And the stranger at Jacob's well said the sentence this Gospel has been building toward since the prologue: “I who speak to you am He.” The first person in John's Gospel to hear Jesus say it outright is a Samaritan woman with five husbands, at noon, at a well.

title: The Fields Are White for Harvest
subtitle: John 4:27–42
description: The woman leaves her jar and evangelizes her town, while Jesus tells his disciples the fields are already ripe.
paragraphs: The disciples came back from town with the food and found their rabbi deep in conversation with a Samaritan woman, and John records their reaction honestly: they were surprised, and none of them said so. No one asked him, “What do You want from her?” or “Why are You talking with her?” Their silence hangs in the story. Hers did not. Then the woman left her water jar, went back into the town, and said to the people, “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” She left behind the jar she had come for, the whole errand forgotten, and went to the town that knew her history best with the one testimony she had: he told me everything I ever did. The town came out to see.

While they were coming, the disciples were urging their teacher to eat. “Rabbi, eat something.” He answered them the way he had answered the woman, in a register they were not hearing: “I have food to eat that you know nothing about.” They took it as literally as she had taken the living water: could someone have brought him food? He explained himself plainly: “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.” Then he pointed their eyes from the road to the fields around Sychar, where the town was already streaming toward them.

“Do you not say, ‘There are still four months until the harvest’? I tell you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest.” The harvest the proverb pushed four months away was walking toward them in the noon light. “Already the reaper draws his wages and gathers a crop for eternal life, so that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together. For in this case the saying ‘One sows and another reaps’ is true. I sent you to reap what you have not worked for; others have done the hard work, and now you have taken up their labor.” Others had sown in Samaria long before this day: Jacob at his well, the prophets, the woman herself in the next ten minutes.

What the disciples were told, the town enacted. Many of the Samaritans from that town believed in Jesus because of the woman's testimony: “He told me everything I ever did.” The Samaritans asked him to stay, the Jew who had asked their outcast for a drink, and he stayed two days, in their town, at their tables. And many more believed because of his message. And the belief outgrew its first witness, exactly as the Baptist's had before her. They said to the woman, “We now believe not only because of your words; we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.” Savior of the world is a title no one in the other accounts gives him this early, and John lets it come from Samaritans, in Samaria, on the word of a woman who could not keep herself from telling what he had told her.

title: Your Son Will Live
subtitle: John 4:43–54
description: A royal official begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son, and takes him at his word across twenty miles.
paragraphs: After two days among the Samaritans, Jesus went on to Galilee, carrying with him his own bleak proverb, which John reports as his own testimony: a prophet has no honor in his own hometown. Yet the Galileans welcomed him, because they had been up to Jerusalem for the feast and had seen what he did there. So he came again to Cana, the village of the water jars, and in Cana he was met by a man with rank and no power at all: a royal official from Herod's court, whose son lay sick at Capernaum, twenty miles away. He had heard that Jesus had come from Judea, and he came and begged him to come down to Capernaum and heal his son, who was about to die.

The answer he got sounds like a rebuff, and it is aimed wider than one father: “Unless you people see signs and wonders, you will never believe.” The official did not defend the people, or himself, or his need for a sign. He just repeated the errand, with the clock in it: “Sir,” the official said, “come down before my child dies.” It is the prayer of a man who is not asking for proof anymore, only for presence, and quickly.

“Go,” said Jesus. “Your son will live.” That was the whole of it. No journey to Capernaum, no touch, no prayer spoken aloud, just a sentence released at Cana while the boy lay dying twenty miles away. John marks what the official did with it, because it is the hinge of the story: “The man took Jesus at His word and departed.” He took him at his word. He walked home at the pace of a man whose request had been granted by a sentence, with nothing to show for it but the sentence.

And while he was still on the way, his servants met him with the news that his boy was alive. The official did what any father with his training would do. He checked the timestamp. So he inquired as to the hour when his son had recovered, and they told him, “The fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour.” Yesterday, at the seventh hour, while he was still pleading at Cana. Then the father realized that this was the very hour in which Jesus had told him, “Your son will live.” The word had traveled faster than the father. Distance, which had been the whole terror of the story, turned out to be nothing to the man who spoke it.

John closes the account with his bookkeeping, the count he has been keeping since the wedding: “This was now the second sign that Jesus performed after coming from Judea into Galilee.” Second sign. And he adds the harvest of it, in the pattern Samaria set: “And he and all his household believed.” A court official's house, twenty miles from the place of speaking, believed because a father took a sentence at face value and walked home to find it true.

title: Rise, Take Up Your Mat
subtitle: John 5:1–18
description: By the pool of Bethesda Jesus heals a man invalid for thirty-eight years, on the Sabbath, and the persecution begins.
paragraphs: Some time later there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem, and John takes the reader to one of the city's saddest addresses. “Now there is in Jerusalem near the Sheep Gate a pool with five covered colonnades, which in Hebrew is called Bethesda.” On its walkways lay a great number of the sick, the blind, the lame, and the paralyzed, a hospital with no doctors, where the healing was rumored to come to the water itself and the quickest body won. One man there had been an invalid for thirty-eight years, longer than Jesus had been alive. When Jesus saw him lying there and realized that he had spent a long time in this condition, he asked him, “Do you want to get well?”

It sounds like a strange question until his answer explains it. “Sir,” the invalid replied, “I have no one to help me into the pool when the water is stirred. While I am on my way, someone else goes in before me.” Thirty-eight years of wanting, and his whole theology of healing was a race he could not run: the water, the stirring, the faster bodies. He did not ask for help. He explained why help had never come. Jesus skipped the water entirely: “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk.” And John records the result with no gap for the man to climb through: “Immediately the man was made well, and he picked up his mat and began to walk.”

Then John drops the sentence the rest of the chapter turns on: “Now this happened on the Sabbath day”. The religious police found the healed man before they found the healer, and their complaint was not about the thirty-eight years. It was about the mat. “This is the Sabbath! It is unlawful for you to carry your mat.” The man gave the only defense he had, which is also the truest summary of the miracle: “The man who made me well told me, ‘Pick up your mat and walk.’” They asked who this man was, and the healed man could not tell them. He did not know his healer's name. Jesus had slipped away into the crowd.

Jesus found him afterward, at the temple, and the second word to him is sterner than the first: “See, you have been made well. Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you.” Something worse than thirty-eight years on a mat is left hanging there, unnamed. The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well, whether in gratitude or defense John does not say, and the information lit the fuse: “Now because Jesus was doing these things on the Sabbath, the Jews began to persecute Him.”

Jesus' answer to the persecution did not lower the temperature. It raised the charge from Sabbath-breaking to something the Sanhedrin would eventually kill him for: “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working.” God works on the Sabbath, sustaining the world he made, and the Son claims the same exemption by birth. John's summary is flat and legal: “Because of this, the Jews tried all the harder to kill Him. Not only was He breaking the Sabbath, but He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God.” The healing by the pool is over. The argument about who Jesus is has begun, and it will run for the rest of the Gospel.

title: The Son Gives Life
subtitle: John 5:19–47
description: Jesus answers the charge of making himself equal with God: the Son gives life, judges, and calls his witnesses.
paragraphs: Jesus answered the charge of making himself equal with God by refusing to be equal in the way they meant, and the answer is the longest sustained claim he has made in the Gospel so far. “Truly, truly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does.” Not independence, but imitation so complete it looks like identity. The Father is not threatened by the Son's works; he shows them to him: “The Father loves the Son and shows Him all He does. And to your amazement, He will show Him even greater works than these.” Greater works than a thirty-eight-year invalid walking. The discourse now names them.

The first is resurrection itself. “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes.” The second is judgment, handed over entire: “Furthermore, the Father judges no one, but has assigned all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him.” And between those two thrones, resurrection and judgment, Jesus sets the door of the whole Gospel open in the present tense: “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life.” Has crossed, already, by hearing and believing.

Then the future crowds into the present. “Truly, truly, I tell you, the hour is coming and has now come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” The Son has life in himself because the Father granted it, and with it the authority to judge, “because He is the Son of Man.” And the voice that wakes the spiritually dead now will one day empty the cemeteries: “Do not be amazed at this, for the hour is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out”, and then the two processions, “those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.”

A claim this size needs witnesses, and Jesus closes the discourse by calling them like a man in court. His own testimony about himself would not count, he concedes, so hear the others. First, John: “You have sent to John, and he has testified to the truth.” Jesus does not need human testimony, he says, but they had embraced the Baptist for a season: “John was a lamp that burned and gave light, and you were willing for a season to bask in his light.” Second, the works themselves: “But I have testimony more substantial than that of John.” The works the Father gave him to finish testify that the Father sent him. Third, the Father, whom they have never heard or seen, whose word does not live in them because they refuse the one he sent.

And last, the witness they trusted most, turned witness for the prosecution. “You pore over the Scriptures because you presume that by them you possess eternal life. These are the very words that testify about Me, yet you refuse to come to Me to have life.” They searched the Scriptures for life and walked past the life the Scriptures described. He will not be their accuser, he tells them. Moses will, the lawgiver they set their hope on: “If you had believed Moses, you would believe Me, because he wrote about Me. But since you do not believe what he wrote, how will you believe what I say?” The discourse ends there, in a courtroom silence, with the pool and the mat far behind and the real charge on the table: not what Jesus did on the Sabbath, but who he is every day of the week.

title: Five Loaves by the Sea
subtitle: John 6:1–21
description: Five barley loaves feed five thousand on the hillside, and that night Jesus walks across the stormy sea to his disciples.
paragraphs: Some time later Jesus crossed to the far shore of the Sea of Galilee, and the crowds followed him around the lake because they had seen the signs he was doing on the sick. Passover was near again. Jesus went up on the mountain and sat down with his disciples, and when he looked up, a great crowd was coming toward him up the slope. He turned to Philip, the disciple from those parts, and asked a question John tells us was a test, because he already knew what he was going to do: “Where can we buy bread for these people to eat?”

Philip did the arithmetic of the empire and it failed immediately: “Two hundred denarii would not buy enough bread for each of them to have a small piece.” Two hundred days' wages, and it would not give the crowd a taste each. Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, the man who kept bringing people, brought forward what he had found, apologizing for it in the same breath: “Here is a boy with five barley loaves and two small fish. But what difference will these make among so many?” Barley was poor people's bread. It was a child's lunch. It was what there was.

Jesus took over with the calm of a host. “Have the people sit down,” Jesus said. There was plenty of grass in that place, and the men sat down, about five thousand of them, not counting whoever else the count left out. “Then Jesus took the loaves and the fish, gave thanks, and distributed to those who were seated as much as they wanted.” As much as they wanted. The test Philip failed with arithmetic was answered with a child's lunch and thanksgiving, and the hillside ate. And when everyone was full, the man who had just multiplied food past counting gave an order about leftovers: “Gather the pieces that are left over, so that nothing will be wasted.” They filled twelve baskets with the pieces of the five barley loaves, one basket, a reader might notice, for each of the Twelve who had said it could not be done.

The crowd drew the conclusion crowds draw from full stomachs. “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world.” And they moved to finish the logic themselves, to come and make him king by force. Jesus realized it and withdrew again to the mountain by himself, leaving the kingship on the hillside with the empty baskets.

That night the disciples went down to the sea without him and started across to Capernaum in the dark. A strong wind rose and the sea grew rough, and three or four miles out, alone in a storming boat, they saw Jesus approaching, walking on the sea, and they were terrified. The figure on the water spoke the smallest possible sermon: “It is I; do not be afraid.” Then they were willing to take him into the boat, John says, “and at once the boat reached the shore where they were heading.” The chapter that began with not enough bread ends with a boat arriving the instant he steps in, and the mountain king they tried to draft is nowhere in it.

title: I Am the Bread of Life
subtitle: John 6:22–51
description: The crowd that ate the loaves demands another sign, and Jesus declares himself the bread that came down from heaven.
paragraphs: The next day the crowd solved the mystery of the missing boat. Only one boat had been on that shore, and Jesus had not gotten into it, yet he was gone. So they got into boats from Tiberias and crossed to Capernaum looking for him, and when they found him, their question was purely logistical: “Rabbi, when did You get here?” Jesus answered the question they had not asked, about why they had really come. “Truly, truly, I tell you, it is not because you saw these signs that you are looking for Me, but because you ate the loaves and had your fill.” They had not seen a sign. They had eaten a meal. “Do not work for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you. For on Him God the Father has placed His seal of approval.”

They asked how to get on the payroll of this lasting food: “What must we do to perform the works of God?” The answer collapsed all their works into one: “The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent.” So they asked for credentials, and the request is brazen on the morning after five thousand people ate from five loaves. “What sign then will You perform, so that we may see it and believe You? What will You do? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, as it is written: ‘He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’” Moses gave daily bread from heaven for forty years, is the argument. Match that.

Jesus corrected their history before he answered their demand. “Truly, truly, I tell you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is He who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.” Not gave, past tense, in the wilderness. Gives, now, and the bread is a person, and the gift is not for Israel's camp but for the world. They rose to it the way the Samaritan woman rose to the living water, on the level of appetite: “Sir,” they said, “give us this bread at all times.”

Then he said the first of this Gospel's great I am sayings to stand alone: “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to Me will never hunger, and whoever believes in Me will never thirst.” And he grieved over them in the same breath: “But as I stated, you have seen Me and still you do not believe.” What he promised next was not that the door would stay open to the striving, but that everyone the Father gives him will come, and “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away.” The will of the Father underneath it all: “that I shall lose none of those He has given Me, but raise them up at the last day. For it is My Father’s will that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in Him shall have eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day.”

The synagogue crowd at Capernaum began to grumble, and their grumble was the local knowledge of Nazareth carried across the lake: “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How then can He say, ‘I have come down from heaven’?” He would not let them murmur in peace: “Stop grumbling among yourselves,” Jesus replied. “No one can come to Me unless the Father who sent Me draws him, and I will raise him up at the last day.” It is written in the Prophets, he told them: “And they will all be taught by God.” Then he said it again, plainer, and pushed it to the edge they would not cross in the next scene: “I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that anyone may eat of it and not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And this bread, which I will give for the life of the world, is My flesh.”

title: Words of Eternal Life
subtitle: John 6:52–71
description: The hard saying about eating his flesh empties the crowd, and Peter confesses there is nowhere else to go.
paragraphs: The word flesh split the synagogue. “How can this man give us His flesh to eat?” the Jews argued among themselves, and Jesus, instead of stepping back from the hard word, stepped further into it. “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you. Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up at the last day. For My flesh is real food, and My blood is real drink.” And the union he promised was the deepest in the Gospel so far: “Whoever eats My flesh and drinks My blood remains in Me, and I in him.” Then he set the manna down for the last time: “This is the bread that came down from heaven. Unlike your fathers, who ate the manna and died, the one who eats this bread will live forever.” All of it, John notes, was said while teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum, in public, on the record.

The offense was not confined to his opponents. On hearing it, many of his disciples said, “This is a difficult teaching. Who can accept it?” His own wider circle of followers was stumbling at the saying. Jesus knew they were grumbling and faced it directly: “Does this offend you? Then what will happen if you see the Son of Man ascend to where He was before?” The flesh language has a direction, and he pointed at it: “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words I have spoken to you are spirit and they are life.” And then the sadness underneath the whole chapter: “However, there are some of you who do not believe.” For Jesus had known from the beginning, John says, which of them did not believe and who would betray him.

What happened next is one of the quiet tragedies of the Gospels, told in a single sentence: “From that time on many of His disciples turned back and no longer walked with Him.” The hillside crowd, the synagogue crowd, the would-be kingmakers, gone. The ministry that had fed five thousand now stood in a room with twelve men, and Jesus turned to them with a question that has the door wide open in it: “Do you want to leave too?”

Simon Peter answered for the Twelve, and his answer is not that the teaching had become easier. “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life. We believe and know that You are the Holy One of God.” To whom would we go. The hard saying had cost them everyone else, and Peter's confession is that there was nowhere else to go, because the words of eternal life were in this room. Jesus received it and dropped a shadow across it that only he could see: “Have I not chosen you, the Twelve? Yet one of you is a devil!” He was speaking about Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, John explains. For although Judas was one of the Twelve, he was later to betray him. The chapter that opened with five thousand fed ends with eleven believers, one devil, and the words of eternal life still standing in the middle of the room.

title: Rivers of Living Water
subtitle: John 7:1–52
description: At the Feast of Tabernacles Jesus teaches in the temple, the crowd divides, the officers return empty-handed, and Nicodemus speaks up.
paragraphs: After Capernaum, Jesus traveled throughout Galilee and stayed out of Judea, because the Jews there were trying to kill him. But the Feast of Tabernacles was near, the autumn festival when Jerusalem filled with pilgrims living in booths, and his own brothers pressed him to go up and perform. “Leave here and go to Judea, so that Your disciples there may see the works You are doing. For no one who wants to be known publicly acts in secret. Since You are doing these things, show Yourself to the world.” It was family advice with an edge, and John underlines why: “For even His own brothers did not believe in Him.”

Jesus refused the schedule they offered him. “I am not going up to this feast, because My time has not yet come.” Their time was always at hand; the world could not hate them, because the world only hates the witness against its works. His time ran on another clock, the hour the prologue's darkness was waiting for. Having said this, he remained in Galilee. But after his brothers had gone up, he also went, not publicly, but in secret, and the feast began with Jerusalem looking for a man who was already there. “Where is He?” the Jews kept asking, and the crowds whispered in both directions at once: “He is a good man.” “No, He deceives the people.” Yet no one would speak publicly about him for fear of the Jews.

About halfway through the feast, Jesus went up to the temple courts and began to teach, openly, in the place he had cleared with a whip two Passovers before. The learning astonished men who knew his schooling, or lack of it: “How did this man attain such learning without having studied?” Jesus answered the question of source the same way he had answered it by the pool: “My teaching is not My own,” Jesus replied. “It comes from Him who sent Me.” And then he gave them the test for it, a test of the will before the mind: anyone who desires to do God's will will know whether the teaching is from God. Then he turned prosecutor: “Has not Moses given you the law? Yet not one of you keeps it. Why are you trying to kill Me?” The crowd, who knew nothing of the plot, answered with the street diagnosis: “You have a demon,” the crowd replied. “Who is trying to kill You?”

He took them back to the one deed that had started the killing talk, the man made well by the pool: “I did one miracle, and you are all amazed.” Moses' own law circumcised a boy on the Sabbath to keep the covenant; “If a boy can be circumcised on the Sabbath so that the law of Moses will not be broken, why are you angry with Me for making the whole man well on the Sabbath? Stop judging by outward appearances, and start judging justly.” The Jerusalemites in the crowd began to see the strangeness of the silence around him: “Isn’t this the man they are trying to kill? Yet here He is, speaking publicly, and they are not saying anything to Him.” Could the rulers have recognized him after all? But the objection of origins rose again: “But we know where this man is from. When the Christ comes, no one will know where He is from.” Jesus, still teaching, cried out over it: “You know Me, and you know where I am from. I have not come of My own accord, but He who sent Me is true. You do not know Him, but I know Him, because I am from Him and He sent Me.” They tried to seize him then, “but no one laid a hand on Him, because His hour had not yet come.” And many in the crowd believed, asking the arithmetic of the signs: “When the Christ comes, will He perform more signs than this man?”

The whispering reached the Pharisees, and officers were sent to arrest him. Jesus spoke as if the arrest were already a date on a calendar he controlled: “I am with you only a little while longer, and then I am going to the One who sent Me. You will look for Me, but you will not find Me; and where I am, you cannot come.” The Jews wondered aloud whether he meant to go and teach the Greeks of the dispersion, a joke history would outrun. Then, on the last and greatest day of the feast, with the water-pouring rite of Tabernacles in every mind, Jesus stood up and called out in a loud voice, not a whisper: “If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink. Whoever believes in Me, as the Scripture has said: ‘Streams of living water will flow from within him.’” John explains what the crowd could not yet know: he was speaking about the Spirit, who would be given after Jesus was glorified.

The crowd split down the middle on the spot. “This is truly the Prophet.” “This is the Christ.” But others objected with their Bibles open: “Doesn’t the Scripture say that the Christ will come from the line of David and from Bethlehem, the village where David lived?” Galilee did not fit their prophecy, and they did not know Bethlehem fit him. There was division in the crowd because of Jesus, and some wanted to seize him, and again no hand landed. The officers came back to the chief priests and Pharisees empty-handed, and when they were asked why they had not brought him in, the arresting party gave the strangest report in the Gospel: “Never has anyone spoken like this man!” The Pharisees cursed the crowd that does not know the law, and then the quiet voice from the night visit spoke up, the only ruler moving toward the light in this chapter: “Does our law convict a man without first hearing from him to determine what he has done?” They sneered him down with geography: “Aren’t you also from Galilee?” they replied. “Look into it, and you will see that no prophet comes out of Galilee.”

title: Neither Do I Condemn You
subtitle: John 7:53–8:11
description: A woman caught in adultery is dragged before Jesus as a test, and her accusers walk away one by one, oldest first.
paragraphs: The council broke up and each man went to his own home, and Jesus went to the Mount of Olives for the night. Early in the morning he was back in the temple courts, and all the people came to him, and he sat down to teach them. Into that quiet classroom the scribes and Pharisees brought their case, and they did not bring it gently: “The scribes and Pharisees, however, brought to Him a woman caught in adultery. They made her stand before them.” Before them, in front of the crowd, a defendant arranged as an exhibit. Her partner is never mentioned. She is the evidence.

“Teacher, this woman was caught in the act of adultery. In the Law Moses commanded us to stone such a woman. So what do You say?” It sounds like a question about law, and John says plainly what it was: “They said this to test Him, in order to have a basis for accusing Him.” If he said stone her, the teacher of mercy would break with Rome's monopoly on execution and with his own reputation in one order. If he said release her, he could be charged with setting himself against Moses. Jesus answered neither way at first. He bent down and began to write on the ground with his finger, the only writing Jesus ever does in any Gospel, and no one tells us what he wrote. They kept questioning him, and the writing stopped, and he straightened up and gave them a courtroom of their own: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her.” Then he bent down and wrote on the ground again.

The stones were never thrown. “When they heard this, they began to go away one by one, beginning with the older ones, until only Jesus was left, with the woman standing there.” The older ones first, a detail with a whole lifetime in it. The accusation drained out of the courtyard in silence, oldest consciences quickest, until the exhibit stood alone before the one man in the place who could have thrown the stone without hypocrisy.

Then Jesus straightened up and asked her, “Woman, where are your accusers? Has no one condemned you?” “No one, Lord,” she answered. She was guilty, and everyone who knew it had left, and the only one left had the right to judge. “Then neither do I condemn you,” Jesus declared. “Now go and sin no more.” Not: it did not matter. Not: they had no case. Neither do I condemn you, and go and sin no more, mercy and command in the same breath, in that order.

One honest line belongs with this story before the next one starts. This account is not found in many of the earliest copies of John's Gospel that survive, and some later copies place it elsewhere. It stands here in the Berean Standard Bible, where the church has read it for centuries, and it is told here as it stands.

title: I Am the Light of the World
subtitle: John 8:12–59
description: In the temple courts Jesus debates his testimony, his father, and Abraham, until he says the words that bring out the stones.
paragraphs: Once again Jesus spoke to the people in the temple courts, near the treasury, where the great lamps of Tabernacles had lit the feast, and gave himself the prologue's own name for him: “I am the light of the world. Whoever follows Me will never walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” The Pharisees answered him as lawyers, not worshipers: “You are testifying about Yourself; Your testimony is not valid.” A man's witness to himself did not count in court, and they meant to keep it a court. Jesus took the rule up and set it aside with knowledge as his credential: “Even if I testify about Myself, My testimony is valid, because I know where I came from and where I am going. But you do not know where I came from or where I am going.” And the second witness their law required stood beside him: “I am One who testifies about Myself, and the Father, who sent Me, also testifies about Me.” “Where is Your Father?” they asked Him. “You do not know Me or My Father,” Jesus answered. “If you knew Me, you would know My Father as well.” No one seized him, John notes again, because his hour had not yet come.

Then the talk darkened into the farewell warnings of the feast. “I am going away, and you will look for Me, but you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come.” They wondered if he meant to kill himself. He told them the distance was not distance but kind: “You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world.” And skipping belief in his signs, his words, his works, he put everything on one clause: “For unless you believe that I am He, you will die in your sins.” “Who are You?” they asked. His answer was a rebuke of the whole conversation: just what I have been telling you from the beginning. And he gave them a sign ahead, the darkest in the chapter, in the Gospel's own code word: “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am He, and that I do nothing on My own, but speak exactly what the Father has taught Me.” As he spoke these things, many believed in him.

To those who had believed, he set the condition that has tested every easy faith since: “If you continue in My word, you are truly My disciples. Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” The free men bristled instantly: “We are Abraham’s descendants,” they answered. “We have never been slaves to anyone. How can You say we will be set free?” Descendants of Abraham, who had been slaves in Egypt, in Babylon, and were subjects of Rome in that very courtyard. Jesus answered in the register of the house, not the empire: “Truly, truly, I tell you, everyone who sins is a slave to sin.” A slave has no permanent place in the house, but a son remains forever: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”

From there the argument went to paternity, and it stopped being polite. They claimed Abraham, then, pressed harder, claimed God: “We are not illegitimate children,” they declared. “Our only Father is God Himself.” Jesus answered with the test of love: “If God were your Father, you would love Me, for I have come here from God. I have not come on My own, but He sent Me.” Actions name the father, he told them, and he named theirs without flinching: “You belong to your father, the devil, and you want to carry out his desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, refusing to uphold the truth, because there is no truth in him.” They answered the light of the world with the street slur of the feast: a Samaritan, demon possessed. He denied the demon, and made the largest promise in the chapter: “Truly, truly, I tell you, if anyone keeps My word, he will never see death.”

“Now we know that You have a demon!” they said, and set the patriarchs against him: “Abraham died, and so did the prophets, yet You say that anyone who keeps Your word will never taste death. Are You greater than our father Abraham? He died, as did the prophets. Who do You claim to be?” His glory, he told them, was his Father's business, the God they claimed and did not know. And then he placed Abraham himself on his side of the argument: “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see My day. He saw it and was glad.” The arithmetic collapsed. “You are not yet fifty years old, and You have seen Abraham?” And Jesus answered with the prologue in two words, the name of God from the burning bush worn as a present tense: “Truly, truly, I tell you,” Jesus declared, “before Abraham was born, I am!” At this they picked up stones to throw at him, there in the temple courts, for blasphemy as they reckoned it. But Jesus was hidden, and went out of the temple area, and the chapter that began with a woman and no stones ends with stones and no victim.

title: One Thing I Know
subtitle: John 9:1–41
description: Jesus gives sight to a man born blind, and the healed beggar out-argues the council that throws him out of the synagogue.
paragraphs: As Jesus was passing by, he saw a man blind from birth, a beggar the disciples had evidently seen before, and they put to him the theology of the street as a question: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” A man born blind could not have earned his darkness, so the sin had to belong to somebody. Jesus refused the whole ledger: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him.” The blindness was not a verdict. It was a canvas. And with the light saying still warm from the temple courts, he claimed it again: “While I am in the world, I am the light of the world.”

Then the light went to work like a laborer. He spit on the ground, made mud with the saliva, and applied it to the man's eyes, and told him, “Go, wash in the Pool of Siloam” (which means Sent). So the man went and washed, blind, groping to the pool with mud on his face, “and came back seeing.” The neighbors and those who had seen him begging began to argue about whether this was even the same man. Some said it was. Others said no, he only looked like him. The man himself settled the identity question with a sentence that echoes the name of God through this whole Gospel: “I am the one.” How were your eyes opened? they asked. He gave them the plainest testimony in the chapter: “The man they call Jesus made some mud and anointed my eyes, and He told me to go to Siloam and wash. So I went and washed and received my sight.” Where is he? “I do not know.”

They brought the man to the Pharisees, and John delivers the fact that organized everything after: the day Jesus made the mud was a Sabbath. The healed man told it again, shorter: “He put mud on my eyes, and I washed, and now I can see.” The council split over the exhibit. “This man is not from God, for He does not keep the Sabbath.” But others said, “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” Division again, in the court itself. They put the question to the one man whose eyes were evidence: “What do you say about Him, since it was your eyes He opened?” “He is a prophet,” the man replied. In one morning the beggar's estimate of Jesus has risen from a name he overheard to a prophet of God, and it will rise twice more before the chapter ends.

The authorities would not take his word for his own blindness. They summoned his parents and cross-examined them: “Is this your son, the one you say was born blind? So how is it that he can now see?” The parents testified to exactly two facts and fled the rest: “We know he is our son, and we know he was born blind. But how he can now see or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him. He is old enough to speak for himself.” John explains their fear without judging it in so many words: the Jews had already determined that anyone who confessed Jesus as the Christ would be put out of the synagogue. To defend their son's healer was to risk their own place in the community of God.

So the man was called a second time, and the court opened with its verdict dressed as an invitation: “Give glory to God! We know that this man is a sinner.” And the beggar gave the answer that has outlived every council: “Whether He is a sinner I do not know. There is one thing I do know: I was blind, but now I see!” They asked the story again, looking for a crack, and he felt the insult of it and answered with a courage his parents had not dared: “I already told you, and you did not listen. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become His disciples?” They heaped insults on him and claimed their own pedigree: “You are His disciple; we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses, but we do not know where this man is from.” Then the uneducated witness stood up in their court and preached the sermon of the chapter: “That is remarkable indeed!” the man said. “You do not know where He is from, and yet He opened my eyes. We know that God does not listen to sinners, but He does listen to the one who worships Him and does His will. Never before has anyone heard of opening the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, He could do no such thing.” They threw him out with the old theology thrown in his face: “You were born in utter sin, and you are instructing us?”

When Jesus heard that they had thrown him out, he went and found him, the second time in this Gospel that Jesus seeks the one the system expelled. “Do you believe in the Son of Man?” “Who is He, Sir?” he replied. “Tell me so that I may believe in Him.” “You have already seen Him,” Jesus answered. “He is the One speaking with you.” “Lord, I believe,” he said. And he worshiped Jesus, this man who had never seen anything at all until that morning, worshiping on sight. Jesus closed the chapter with the reversal the whole story had been performing: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that the blind may see and those who see may become blind.” Some Pharisees standing by heard it and asked, stung, “Are we blind too?” “If you were blind,” Jesus replied, “you would not be guilty of sin. But since you claim you can see, your guilt remains.”

title: I Am the Good Shepherd
subtitle: John 10:1–21
description: Jesus pictures the sheepfold: thieves climb the wall, but the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
paragraphs: Jesus did not leave the expelled beggar or his expellers without a picture to think in, and the picture is a sheepfold at night. “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever does not enter the sheepfold by the gate, but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber.” The man who comes over the wall comes for the sheep, not for their good. The shepherd comes through the gate, in the open, and the gatekeeper opens for him, “and the sheep listen for his voice. He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.” He does not drive them from behind. He goes ahead of them, and they follow the one sound in the world they trust: “But they will never follow a stranger; in fact, they will flee from him because they do not recognize his voice.” Jesus spoke this illustration to them, John says, and they did not understand what he was telling them.

So he named himself in it twice. First as the door the wall-climbers will not use: “Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the gate for the sheep.” All who came before him with claims were thieves and robbers, and the sheep had not listened. “I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved. He will come in and go out and find pasture.” Against every thief in the picture he set the purpose of his own coming, in one of the Gospel's great sentences: “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy. I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness.”

Then he named himself as the shepherd, and the picture turned from entry to death. “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.” The test of a shepherd, in this telling, is the wolf. “The hired hand is not the shepherd, and the sheep are not his own. When he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away.” Wages cannot make a man die for sheep that are not his, and Jesus is blunt about why the hireling runs: he is unconcerned for the sheep. The good shepherd is known by the opposite marks, knowledge and the grave: “I am the good shepherd. I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father. And I lay down My life for the sheep.”

And the fold is bigger than the one in front of him: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them in as well, and they will listen to My voice. Then there will be one flock and one shepherd.” Samaritans had already heard that voice. The world would. Then he said the thing that separates his death from every martyrdom: “The reason the Father loves Me is that I lay down My life in order to take it up again. No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord. I have authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. This charge I have received from My Father.”

Again there was division among the Jews because of his message. The two verdicts of the whole Gospel stand side by side in one verse pair. “He is demon-possessed and insane. Why would you listen to Him?” But others replied, “These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” The man born blind, thrown out of the synagogue that morning, had become the evidence no one in the argument could answer.

title: My Sheep Hear My Voice
subtitle: John 10:22–42
description: At the Feast of Dedication Jesus says, I and the Father are one, escapes the stones, and withdraws across the Jordan.
paragraphs: At that time the Feast of Dedication took place in Jerusalem, the winter festival of the temple's rededication, and it was winter. Jesus was walking in the temple courts in Solomon's Colonnade, under cover from the cold, when the Jews gathered around him and demanded the plain speech they had been wanting since the feast of Tabernacles: “How long will You keep us in suspense? If You are the Christ, tell us plainly.”

“I already told you,” Jesus replied, “but you did not believe. The works I do in My Father’s name testify on My behalf.” He had told them with a healed invalid, a fed multitude, a blind man's opened eyes. The problem was not information, and he named it without cushion: they did not believe because they were not his sheep. His sheep know his voice the way the fold knows the shepherd at the gate: “My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish. No one can snatch them out of My hand.” And behind his hand, a greater: “My Father who has given them to Me is greater than all. No one can snatch them out of My Father’s hand.” Then, in Solomon's Colonnade, with the winter crowd pressing in, he said the sentence the whole Gospel had been circling since its first verse: “I and the Father are one.”

At this, the Jews again picked up stones to stone him, and Jesus did something unexpected in the moment before a stoning. He asked them to specify the capital charge by exhibit: “I have shown you many good works from the Father. For which of these do you stone Me?” They answered with perfect clarity about what the argument had always been: “We are not stoning You for any good work,” said the Jews, “but for blasphemy, because You, who are a man, make Yourself out to be God.”

His answer went to their own Scriptures, to a psalm where God calls Israel's judges gods: “Is it not written in your Law: ‘I have said you are gods’?” If the word of God could call mere men gods, and the Scripture cannot be broken, how is it blasphemy when the One the Father sanctified and sent into the world calls himself the Son of God? Then he fell back on the offer he had made all chapter, belief by evidence if not by word: “But if I am doing them, even though you do not believe Me, believe the works themselves, so that you may know and understand that the Father is in Me, and I am in the Father.” At this they tried again to seize him, but he escaped their grasp, out of the temple, out of the city, out of reach until his hour.

He went back across the Jordan to the place where John had first been baptizing, the place of the Lamb of God and the descending dove, and there the crowds came to him with the Baptist's vindication on their lips: “Although John never performed a sign, everything he said about this man was true.” John had done no miracle. He had only pointed, and years later the pointing was still gathering people. “And many in that place believed in Jesus.” The witness was in prison or dead by now, and his testimony was still doing its work in the place where it started.

title: I Am the Resurrection and the Life
subtitle: John 11:1–27
description: Word comes that Lazarus is sick; Jesus waits two days, then meets Martha on the road outside Bethany.
paragraphs: At this time a man named Lazarus was sick, in Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha, less than two miles from Jerusalem. John stops to identify Mary by something she has not done yet in his telling: she is the one whose brother Lazarus was sick, the Mary who would anoint the Lord with perfume and wipe his feet with her hair. The sisters sent word to Jesus, and the message they sent is a whole theology of friendship in seven words: “Lord, the one You love is sick.” No request, no instructions, just the fact laid before love, the way his mother once laid the empty wine jars before him at Cana.

Jesus received the message and pronounced the end of the story at its beginning: “This sickness will not end in death. No, it is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.” Then John writes the sentence that makes the next move so strange: “Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So on hearing that Lazarus was sick, He stayed where He was for two days”. Loved them, so he stayed. The delay is not explained, and anyone who has prayed over a sickbed knows the shape of those two days. When they passed, he said to the disciples, “Let us go back to Judea.”

They protested on recent evidence: “Rabbi,” they replied, “the Jews just tried to stone You, and You are going back there?” Jesus answered them with the riddle of the working day: “Are there not twelve hours of daylight? If anyone walks in the daytime, he will not stumble, because he sees by the light of this world. But if anyone walks at night, he will stumble, because he has no light.” Then he told them the errand in a figure: “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I am going there to wake him up.” They took it as the best news possible: “Lord, if he is sleeping, he will get better.” John explains the misunderstanding for the reader, that Jesus was speaking of death, and then Jesus dropped the figure entirely: “Lazarus is dead, and for your sake I am glad I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.” Glad, for their sakes, at the fact of his friend's death, because of what they were about to see. Thomas, called Didymus, turned to his fellow disciples and said the bravest gloomy sentence in the Gospel: “Let us also go, so that we may die with Him.”

When Jesus arrived, he found that Lazarus had already spent four days in the tomb. Bethany was crowded with comforters from Jerusalem who had come to console the sisters. When Martha heard Jesus was coming, she went out to meet him on the road, while Mary stayed at home, and the first words out of her are the words this whole story was written to answer: “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” It is faith and accusation in one sentence, and she followed it immediately with a faith that would not let go: “But even now I know that God will give You whatever You ask of Him.” “Your brother will rise again,” Jesus told her. Martha replied with the creed of her people, correct and cold at a graveside: “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection at the last day.”

Jesus took the resurrection out of the last day and put it in his own person, standing on the road in front of her: “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies. And everyone who lives and believes in Me will never die. Do you believe this?” Not do you understand it. Do you believe it. And Martha, who has been the practical sister in every story, made the fullest confession anyone has made in this Gospel: “Yes, Lord,” she answered, “I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who was to come into the world.” Peter's confession at Capernaum named him the Holy One of God. Martha's names him Christ and Son of God, at a tomb, before she has seen a single thing happen.

title: Jesus Wept
subtitle: John 11:28–57
description: At the tomb Jesus weeps, calls Lazarus out of the grave, and the Sanhedrin resolves that one man must die for the nation.
paragraphs: Martha went back to the house and called her sister aside with the news in a whisper: “The Teacher is here and is asking for you.” Mary got up quickly and went out, and the mourners followed her, supposing she was going to the tomb to mourn there, a whole procession arriving at the wrong destination with the right person.
