Mary came to the place where Martha had met him and fell at his feet with her sister's exact sentence on her lips: “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” Then she wept, and the Jews who had come with her wept, and John gives the reaction of Jesus in the rawest words of his Gospel: “He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled.” The word carries indignation in it, a snort of anger at death itself, and no one who reads the scene at a graveside should smooth it down. “Where have you put him?” He asked. “Come and see, Lord,” they answered.

“Jesus wept.” It is the shortest verse in the Bible and it stands in the story like a stone. He knew he was about to raise the man. He had said the sickness would end in glory. And standing at the tomb of his friend, with the sisters weeping around him, he wept anyway. The Jews read the tears two ways, the way crowds always read him. “See how He loved him!” And some of them asked, with the blind man's story still current: “Could not this man who opened the eyes of the blind also have kept Lazarus from dying?”

Deeply moved again, Jesus came to the tomb, a cave with a stone laid across the entrance, and gave the order that set everyone's nerves on edge: “Take away the stone,” Jesus said. Martha, the sister of the dead man, practical to the last, said what everyone was thinking: “Lord, by now he stinks,” said Martha. “It has already been four days.” Jesus replied with the promise he had given her on the road: “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” So they took away the stone.

Then Jesus lifted his eyes and prayed aloud, and the prayer itself explains that it is not for his benefit: “Father, I thank You that You have heard Me. I knew that You always hear Me, but I say this for the benefit of the people standing here, so they may believe that You sent Me.” After he had said this, he called out in a loud voice, the voice the sheep know, aimed at a cave: “Lazarus, come out!” And the man who had been dead came out, with his hands and feet bound in strips of linen, and his face wrapped in a cloth, alive inside his own grave clothes. “Unwrap him and let him go,” Jesus told them. The last work of the miracle was given to the mourners' hands.

Many of the Jews who had come to Mary believed in him because of what they saw. But some of them went to the Pharisees and reported it, and the miracle landed in the Sanhedrin as a political emergency: “What are we to do? This man is performing many signs. If we let Him go on like this, everyone will believe in Him, and then the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.” The dead man walking had become, in the council's arithmetic, a threat to the temple and the nation. Caiaphas, high priest that year, cut through them with the year's coldest sentence: “You know nothing at all! You do not realize that it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish.” John stops the story to tell the reader that the high priest had prophesied better than he knew, that Jesus would die for the nation, “and not only for the nation, but also for the scattered children of God, to gather them together into one.” So from that day on they plotted to kill him, and Jesus withdrew to Ephraim near the wilderness, and the orders went out that anyone who knew where he was must report it. Passover was near, and all Jerusalem was asking one question in the temple courts: “What do you think? Will He come to the feast at all?”

title: Mary Anointed His Feet
subtitle: John 12:1–19
description: Mary anoints Jesus' feet with costly perfume, the crowds come to see Lazarus too, and Jesus enters Jerusalem on a donkey.
paragraphs: Six days before the Passover, Jesus came back to Bethany, the hometown of Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead, with the arrest orders still out and the feast six days away. They hosted a dinner for him there. Martha served, as she always served, and Lazarus was among those reclining at the table with him, the dead man at dinner, eating. It is one of the strangest guest lists in the Bible and John offers it without blinking.

Then Mary took about a pint of expensive perfume, made of pure nard, “and she anointed Jesus’ feet and wiped them with her hair.” Not his head, as a host honors a guest. His feet, with her hair let down in company, a woman's glory used as a towel for the dirtiest part of a traveler. “And the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.” John remembers the smell of it years later. But one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was going to betray him, put a price on the act: “Why wasn’t this perfume sold for three hundred denarii and the money given to the poor?” Three hundred denarii, a workingman's year. John, who knows the end of Judas's story, will not let the piety stand unexamined: Judas did not say it because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, keeper of the money bag who helped himself to what was put in it.

“Leave her alone,” Jesus replied. “She has kept this perfume in preparation for the day of My burial. The poor you will always have with you, but you will not always have Me.” She has kept it for the burial. Mary, who sat at his feet to listen and fell at his feet to weep, understood the week she was in better than the man counting the money. The poor would always be there to be helped. He would not.

Meanwhile a large crowd of Jews learned that Jesus was there, and they came not only because of him, but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. The miracle had become a sight to see on the road to the feast. And the Sanhedrin's arithmetic absorbed the new fact with terrible logic: “So the chief priests made plans to kill Lazarus as well, for on account of him many of the Jews were deserting them and believing in Jesus.” The man death could not hold was to be killed for the evidence of being alive. John states it flatly and moves on, and the flatness is the indictment.

The next day the great crowd that had come to the feast heard Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, and they took palm branches and went out to meet him, shouting the psalm of the coming king: “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the King of Israel!” Finding a young donkey, Jesus sat on it, as it is written: “Do not be afraid, O Daughter of Zion. See, your King is coming, seated on the colt of a donkey.” A king on a donkey, entering his city to the sound of a crowd that wanted a throne, six days from a cross. His disciples did not understand these things at the time, John admits; only after Jesus was glorified did they remember what had been done, and realize it had been written. The crowd that had watched Lazarus come out of the tomb kept testifying, and that testimony is why the city poured out to meet him. Then the Pharisees said to one another, in the despair of men watching their arithmetic fail: “You can see that this is doing you no good. Look how the whole world has gone after Him!”

title: The Hour Has Come
subtitle: John 12:20–50
description: Greeks ask to see Jesus, a voice speaks from heaven, and John's Gospel closes out the public ministry with Isaiah's audit.
paragraphs: Now there were some Greeks among those who went up to worship at the feast, God-fearers from the wider world, and they came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, with a request that sounds small and changes everything: “Sir, we want to see Jesus.” Philip relayed the appeal to Andrew, and both of them went and told Jesus. Foreigners at the door, wanting to see him. Jesus answered Andrew and Philip with the sentence his whole Gospel has been holding back since the wedding at Cana, when his hour had not yet come: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” The world was arriving, and the arrival set the hour.

And the glory, when he explained it, was a burial: “Truly, truly, I tell you, unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a seed. But if it dies, it bears much fruit.” The harvest of the world required the seed in the ground. The law of it applied to his followers as to him: “Whoever loves his life will lose it, but whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.” Then his soul showed the strain that John's Gospel never hides: “Now My soul is troubled, and what shall I say? ‘Father, save Me from this hour’? No, it is for this purpose that I have come to this hour. Father, glorify Your name!” There is John's Gethsemane, out loud, in public, in two sentences. And heaven answered it audibly. Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” The crowd standing there heard it and said it had thundered. Others said an angel had spoken to him. Jesus told them the voice had not been for his benefit but for theirs.

“Now judgment is upon this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everyone to Myself.” John pauses to make sure the reader does not miss the code he has been using since Nicodemus: he said this to indicate the kind of death he was going to die. Lifted up means the cross, and the cross is the magnet. The crowd had done its theology and found the contradiction: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ will remain forever. So how can You say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?” A Messiah who remains forever does not get lifted up to die. Jesus did not resolve their chart. He warned them about the light: “For a little while longer, the Light will be among you. Walk while you have the Light, so that darkness will not overtake you.” “While you have the Light, believe in the Light, so that you may become sons of light.” After he had spoken these things, he went away and was hidden from them. The public teaching of John's Gospel ends there, a few sentences from the Greeks who started it.

John closes the ministry with an audit, and it is bleak: “Although Jesus had performed so many signs in their presence, they still did not believe in Him.” He reaches for Isaiah twice to explain it, the prophet who saw Jesus' glory and spoke of him: “Lord, who has believed our message? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” And harder: “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their hearts, so that they cannot see with their eyes, and understand with their hearts, and turn, and I would heal them.” And yet the unbelief was not total, only silent: “Nevertheless, many of the leaders believed in Him. But because of the Pharisees they did not confess Him, for fear that they would be put out of the synagogue. For they loved praise from men more than praise from God.” Nicodemus's disease, diagnosed at last.

Then, hidden though he was, Jesus cried out one final summary of everything, and it is fitting that the last public words of this Gospel's ministry are about seeing and believing the Sender in the Son: “Whoever believes in Me does not believe in Me alone, but in the One who sent Me. And whoever sees Me sees the One who sent Me. I have come into the world as a light, so that no one who believes in Me should remain in darkness.” He had not come to judge the world but to save it; the word he spoke would be judge enough on the last day. “And I know that His command leads to eternal life. So I speak exactly what the Father has told Me to say.”

title: He Loved Them to the End
subtitle: John 13:1–38
description: At the last supper Jesus washes his disciples' feet, gives the morsel to Judas, and tells Peter about the rooster.
paragraphs: It was now just before the Passover Feast, and Jesus knew that his hour had come to leave this world and return to the Father. John states the fact and then states the love that governed everything done inside it: “Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the very end.” The evening meal was underway, and the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him. And Jesus knew that the Father had delivered all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was returning to God. It is with all things in his hands that he does the next thing.

“So He got up from the supper, laid aside His outer garments, and wrapped a towel around His waist. After that, He poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and dry them with the towel that was around Him.” The master dressed as the household slave, on his knees, with a basin, working his way around the table of men who had argued about greatness. He came to Simon Peter, who asked him, “Lord, are You going to wash my feet?” Jesus replied, “You do not realize now what I am doing, but later you will understand.” Peter refused the basin outright: “Never shall You wash my feet!” Jesus answered with the stakes of the towel: “Unless I wash you, you have no part with Me.” Peter swung the way Peter always swung, all the way over: “Then, Lord,” Simon Peter replied, “not only my feet, but my hands and my head as well!” Jesus told him the bath was already given; only the feet of the road need washing, “And you are clean, though not all of you.” For he knew who would betray him. That is why he said not all of them were clean. One pair of feet at that table was already walking somewhere else in its heart, and Jesus washed them anyway.

When he had put on his garments and reclined again, he interpreted the act himself: “Do you know what I have done for you? You call Me Teacher and Lord, and rightly so, because I am. So if I, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also should wash one another’s feet. I have set you an example so that you should do as I have done for you.” And the blessing was not in the knowing: “Truly, truly, I tell you, no servant is greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.” Then the table's shadow fell across the teaching: “I am not speaking about all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But this is to fulfill the Scripture: ‘The one who shares My bread has lifted up his heel against Me.’” He told them before it happened, he said, so that when it came to pass they would believe that I am He.

After he had said this, Jesus became troubled in spirit and testified plainly: “Truly, truly, I tell you, one of you will betray Me.” The disciples looked at one another, perplexed, and Simon Peter motioned to the disciple whom Jesus loved, reclining at his side, to ask who it was. Leaning back against Jesus, he asked, “Lord, who is it?” Jesus answered, “It is the one to whom I give this morsel after I have dipped it.” Then he dipped the morsel and gave it to Judas son of Simon Iscariot, the morsel of honor at the meal, from the host's own hand. And when Judas had taken it, Satan entered into him, and Jesus said to him the only command Judas obeyed that night: “What you are about to do, do quickly.” No one at the table understood; since Judas kept the money bag, some thought he was being sent to buy for the feast or to give to the poor. As soon as he had received the morsel, Judas went out. And John closes the exit in four words that carry the whole Gospel's imagery with them: it was night.

When Judas had gone out, Jesus spoke as if a weight had lifted: “Now the Son of Man is glorified, and God is glorified in Him. If God is glorified in Him, God will also glorify the Son in Himself”, and will glorify him at once. Then the tenderness of the farewell broke through: “Little children, I am with you only a little while longer.” And he gave them the commandment by which the world would identify them when he was gone: “A new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another. By this everyone will know that you are My disciples, if you love one another.” Simon Peter asked where he was going, and was told he could not follow now, but would follow later, and Peter made his great vow: “Lord,” said Peter, “why can’t I follow You now? I will lay down my life for You.” Jesus answered the vow with the night's last prophecy: “Will you lay down your life for Me?” Jesus replied. “Truly, truly, I tell you, before the rooster crows, you will deny Me three times.”

title: I Am the Way
subtitle: John 14:1–31
description: The farewell begins: many rooms, the way and the truth and the life, another Advocate, and a peace the world cannot give.
paragraphs: The farewell begins with a command against the night's weather: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe in Me as well.” The betrayer had left. The denial had been predicted. And Jesus spent his last evening giving the eleven reasons not to be afraid, beginning with a house. “In My Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you?” The going away was not abandonment; it was advance work, and it ended in return: “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and welcome you into My presence, so that you also may be where I am. You know the way to the place where I am going.”

Thomas, who would have died with him an hour before and would demand the wounds later, spoke the confusion honestly: “Lord,” said Thomas, “we do not know where You are going, so how can we know the way?” And Jesus answered him with the saying that stands at the center of this Gospel's claims: “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.” Not a map but a person. And the seeing the Father they kept asking for had already been given: “If you had known Me, you would know My Father as well. From now on you do know Him and have seen Him.”

Philip asked for the vision anyway, the way men ask for one more proof: “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.” The sadness in the reply is centuries deep and personal: “Philip, I have been with you all this time, and still you do not know Me? Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father.” The words he spoke were the Father's works being done from inside him. “Believe Me that I am in the Father and the Father is in Me”, he said, and if that was too much, then at least “believe on account of the works themselves.” And then the promise that has startled readers ever since: “Truly, truly, I tell you, whoever believes in Me will also do the works that I am doing. He will do even greater things than these, because I am going to the Father. And I will do whatever you ask in My name, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son.”

Love, in this farewell, is measured by keeping his commandments, and love is answered by a gift: “And I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate to be with you forever”, “the Spirit of truth. The world cannot receive Him, because it neither sees Him nor knows Him. But you do know Him, for He abides with you and will be in you.” Another Advocate, one like Jesus himself, to stay when Jesus leaves. The leaving itself he refused to name as orphaning: “I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you.” And the life on the far side of it: “Because I live, you also will live. On that day you will know that I am in My Father, and you are in Me, and I am in you.”

Judas, not Iscariot, John is careful to say, asked why the revealing was for them and not the world. The answer was the home God makes in the obedient: “If anyone loves Me, he will keep My word. My Father will love him, and We will come to him and make Our home with him.” The many rooms had come down to earth. And because the night itself would scatter their memories, the Advocate had a second errand: “But the Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in My name, will teach you all things and will remind you of everything I have told you.” Then he left them his own possession as a bequest: “Peace I leave with you; My peace I give to you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled; do not be afraid.”

He told them to rejoice at the going, hard as that was, “because the Father is greater than I”, and that everything had been said beforehand so that when it happened they would believe. The talk was ending. “I will not speak with you much longer, for the prince of this world is coming, and he has no claim on Me.” No claim, no charge that would stick; the obedience was the love of the Father made visible. And the discourse that sounded like an ending moved its feet: “Get up! Let us go on from here.” They rose from the table and went out toward the garden, still talking as they went.

title: I Am the True Vine
subtitle: John 15:1–27
description: On the road to the garden Jesus pictures the vine and the branches, renames servants as friends, and warns of the world's hatred.
paragraphs: Somewhere on the walk from the upper room toward the garden, or still at its doorway, Jesus gave the eleven the picture the rest of the night would grow in: “I am the true vine, and My Father is the keeper of the vineyard. He cuts off every branch in Me that bears no fruit, and every branch that does bear fruit, He prunes to make it even more fruitful.” Israel had been God's vine for a thousand years in the Scriptures, and had so often failed to bear. This vine is true. And the Father's knife works two ways only: barren branches are cut off, and fruitful ones are cut back, pruned so they bear more. Even the cutting is a kind of care. “You are already clean,” he told them, “because of the word I have spoken to you.”

Then the word the whole picture hangs on, said four ways so it cannot be missed: “Remain in Me, and I will remain in you. Just as no branch can bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, neither can you bear fruit unless you remain in Me.” “I am the vine and you are the branches. The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing.” The alternative is withering, gathering, and fire. But the promise for those who remain is prayer with the words of the vine living in them: “If you remain in Me and My words remain in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. This is to My Father’s glory, that you bear much fruit, proving yourselves to be My disciples.”

The love that runs in the vine has one channel, and it is the commandment of the supper table: “As the Father has loved Me, so have I loved you. Remain in My love.” “This is My commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends.” He was hours from proving the sentence in his own body. And the men he said it to were renamed in the same breath: “You are My friends if you do what I command you. No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you.” Chosen, too, before they ever chose: “You did not choose Me, but I chose you.” Appointed to go and bear fruit that remains, “so that whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you. This is My command to you: Love one another.” The discourse keeps circling back to the command, as if it were the one thing they must not drop on the road to the garden.

Then the warning side of the choosing: “If the world hates you, understand that it hated Me first.” The world loves its own; these men had been chosen out of it, and the hatred would be transferred like a debt to their account. “Remember the word that I spoke to you: ‘No servant is greater than his master.’ If they persecuted Me, they will persecute you as well; if they kept My word, they will keep yours as well.” His coming had removed the world's excuse: had he not come and spoken, had he not done the works no one else did, they would not be guilty of this sin. Now they had seen, and hated both him and his Father, fulfilling their own Law's cold line: “But this is to fulfill what is written in their Law: ‘They hated Me without reason.’”

Against the hatred stands the witness. “When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father”, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, “He will testify about Me. And you also must testify, because you have been with Me from the beginning.” Two testimonies, the Spirit's and the apostles', and the second one rests on a simple qualification: they had been with him from the beginning, from the Jordan and the fig tree and the wine jars, all the way to this road in the dark.

title: When the Helper Comes
subtitle: John 16:1–33
description: The farewell ends with sorrow turned to joy, the promise of plain speech, and a victory spoken in the past tense.
paragraphs: The last talk on the road opens with its purpose stated: “I have told you these things so that you will not fall away. They will put you out of the synagogues. In fact, a time is coming when anyone who kills you will think he is offering a service to God.” The expulsion the blind man's parents had feared was now forecast for the apostles themselves, and worse, murder done as worship. He had not told them from the beginning, because he was with them and the blows fell on him. Now they were told in advance for one reason: “But I have told you these things so that when their hour comes, you will remember that I told you about them.” Forewarning was his parting gift, so the worst night of their lives would arrive with his voice already inside it.

Yet none of them asked where he was going; sorrow had filled their hearts and stopped the questions. So he gave them the hardest logic of the farewell: “But I tell you the truth, it is for your benefit that I am going away. Unless I go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you.” His absence was the Spirit's arrival condition. And the Spirit's work, when he came, would be a prosecution of the whole world: “And when He comes, He will convict the world in regard to sin and righteousness and judgment: in regard to sin, because they do not believe in Me; in regard to righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you will no longer see Me; and in regard to judgment, because the prince of this world has been condemned.”

There was more truth than they could carry that night, and he refused to overload them with it: “I still have much to tell you, but you cannot yet bear to hear it. However, when the Spirit of truth comes, He will guide you into all truth.” The Spirit would not freelance. “He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you.” Everything the Father has is the Son's; everything the Son's, the Spirit would deliver. The teaching ministry of Jesus was not ending on this road. It was changing hands.

Then the riddle that tangled them one last time: “In a little while you will see Me no more, and then after a little while you will see Me.” They turned it over among themselves, and he answered the question behind it with the picture of a birth: “Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and wail while the world rejoices. You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy. A woman has pain in childbirth because her time has come; but when she brings forth her child, she forgets her anguish because of her joy that a child has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy.” And in that day of seeing, their prayers would run on the new road he had opened: “Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you. Until now you have not asked for anything in My name. Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.”

“I have spoken these things to you in figures of speech. An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you this way, but will tell you plainly about the Father.” And the ground of the new plainness is the Father's own heart, stated without a middleman: “For the Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and entered the world. In turn, I will leave the world and go to the Father.” The disciples seized on the summary: “See, now You are speaking plainly and without figures of speech. Now we understand that You know all things and that You have no need for anyone to question You. Because of this, we believe that You came from God.”

“Do you finally believe?” Jesus replied. It is the gentlest puncturing in the Gospel. “Look, an hour is coming and has already come when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and you will leave Me all alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me.” Their confession would last a few hours; his solitude was already a fellowship. And the discourse, the longest in the Gospels, closes with the reason it was spoken at all: “I have told you these things so that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!” The tribulation is promised in the same breath as the victory, and the victory is in the past tense before the cross. Then he lifted his eyes to heaven and began to pray.

title: Father, Glorify Your Son
subtitle: John 17:1–26
description: Jesus prays aloud for himself, for the eleven, and for everyone who will ever believe through their message.
paragraphs: When Jesus had spoken these things, he lifted up his eyes to heaven and prayed aloud, in the hearing of the men the prayer was mostly about. It is the longest prayer of Jesus any Gospel kept, and it begins where the discourses began, with the hour: “Father, the hour has come. Glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You.” The glory he asks for is the cross, and its purpose is a gift: the authority over all people, to give eternal life to all those the Father has given him. And he defines eternal life, the phrase that has run through the Gospel, as knowing, not merely lasting: “Now this is eternal life, that they may know You, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom You have sent.” Then the report of the finished work, spoken before the work was finished: “I have glorified You on earth by accomplishing the work You gave Me to do. And now, Father, glorify Me in Your presence with the glory I had with You before the world existed.” The prologue's first verse stands up in the prayer: the glory before the world existed.

Then he prayed for the eleven, as a man settling his affairs in the open. “I have revealed Your name to those You have given Me out of the world. They were Yours; You gave them to Me, and they have kept Your word.” The words had been delivered and received: “For I have given them the words You gave Me, and they have received them. They knew with certainty that I came from You, and they believed that You sent Me.” Whatever their failures that night, this was the record their teacher filed for them before the scattering.

His petitions for them are protection, not escape. “I ask on their behalf. I do not ask on behalf of the world, but on behalf of those You have given Me; for they are Yours.” “Holy Father, protect them by Your name, the name You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one.” While he was with them, he had protected and preserved them by that name, and the audit is honest about the one exception: “Not one of them has been lost, except the son of destruction, so that the Scripture would be fulfilled.” And the saying of it aloud had its own purpose: “But now I am coming to You; and I am saying these things while I am in the world, so that they may have My joy fulfilled within them.”

The world had hated them because they were not of it, as he was not of it. He did not ask for their removal from it: “I am not asking that You take them out of the world, but that You keep them from the evil one.” They were to stay, and to be set apart inside the staying: “Sanctify them by the truth; Your word is truth.” Their mission ran on the pattern of his: “As You sent Me into the world, I have also sent them into the world. For them I sanctify Myself, so that they too may be sanctified by the truth.” He sets himself apart to the death ahead, for their sakes, by name.

Then the prayer reached past the garden, past the century, past every reader who has ever heard it and realized it has come to them: “I am not asking on behalf of them alone, but also on behalf of those who will believe in Me through their message, that all of them may be one, as You, Father, are in Me, and I am in You.” The unity asked for is not organization but indwelling, given glory as its bond: “I have given them the glory You gave Me, so that they may be one as We are one”, “that they may be perfectly united, so that the world may know that You sent Me and have loved them just as You have loved Me.” And the prayer's last desire is the house with many rooms, spoken to the Father directly: “Father, I want those You have given Me to be with Me where I am, that they may see the glory You gave Me because You loved Me before the foundation of the world.” It closes where it opened, with the name made known: “Righteous Father, although the world has not known You, I know You, and they know that You sent Me. And I have made Your name known to them and will continue to make it known, so that the love You have for Me may be in them, and I in them.”

title: The Garden Arrest
subtitle: John 18:1–27
description: In the garden Jesus steps forward and is bound; inside Annas's courtyard, Peter warms himself and denies him three times.
paragraphs: After Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the Kidron Valley, where they entered a garden. There is no agony in John's account of that garden, no prayer for the cup to pass, no sleeping friends rebuked. What John gives instead is a king walking to meet his arrest. Judas his betrayer knew the place, because Jesus had often met there with his disciples, and Judas brought a band of soldiers and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, carrying lanterns, torches, and weapons, a small army hunting one unarmed man by torchlight.

Jesus, knowing all that was coming upon him, stepped forward and asked them, “Whom are you seeking?” “Jesus of Nazareth,” they answered. And Jesus gave them the name of God as his answer, I am he. And Judas his betrayer was standing there with them. When Jesus said it, they drew back and fell to the ground, Roman soldiers and temple officers on their backs in the dirt before the man they came to chain. He asked them again whom they sought, and again they said Jesus of Nazareth, and he answered the second time with his condition: “I told you that I am He,” Jesus replied. “So if you are looking for Me, let these men go.” The shepherd of chapter ten, laying down his life of his own accord, first bargaining his captors out of his flock. John says it fulfilled his own word: he had not lost one of those the Father gave him.

Then Simon Peter drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his right ear. The servant's name was Malchus; John, alone of the Gospels, knows both the swordsman and the wounded man's names. Jesus stopped the war Peter tried to start: “Put your sword back in its sheath!” Jesus said to Peter. “Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?” Then the band of soldiers, with its commander and the officers of the Jews, arrested Jesus and bound him, and the man at whose word they had fallen down let them tie his hands.

They brought him first to Annas, the power behind the priesthood, father-in-law of Caiaphas, the high priest that year, the same Caiaphas who had advised that one man should die for the people. Meanwhile Peter followed, with another disciple who was known to the high priest and got him into the courtyard, and at the door the first question found Peter, from a servant girl watching the gate: “Aren’t you also one of this man’s disciples?” He answered that he was not. In the garden, Jesus had said I am, and soldiers fell. In the courtyard, Peter said I am not, and stood warming himself at a charcoal fire with the servants and officers, because it was cold.

Inside, the high priest questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching, and Jesus answered with the openness of his whole ministry: “I have spoken openly to the world,” Jesus answered. “I always taught in the synagogues and at the temple, where all the Jews come together. I said nothing in secret. Why are you asking Me? Ask those who heard My message. Surely they know what I said.” One of the officers standing nearby slapped him in the face for it: “Is this how You answer the high priest?” Jesus replied with the logic of a man who will not bend: “If I said something wrong, testify as to what was wrong. But if I spoke correctly, why did you strike Me?” Annas sent him, still bound, to Caiaphas.

And Peter was still standing and warming himself, and they asked him again: “Aren’t you also one of His disciples?” He denied it again: he was not. Then one of the high priest's servants, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked the question with the garden in it: “Didn’t I see you with Him in the garden?” Peter denied it once more, and immediately a rooster crowed. John does not record Jesus turning to look at him. He does not record Peter weeping. He records the denial, the crow, and the silence after, and moves the bound prisoner toward the Romans.

title: What Is Truth?
subtitle: John 18:28–19:16
description: Before Pilate, Jesus speaks of a kingdom not of this world, is flogged and mocked, and is handed over when the priests claim Caesar.
paragraphs: Then they led Jesus away from Caiaphas into the Praetorium, the Roman governor's headquarters, and John's eye catches the detail that condemns the whole proceeding before it starts: it was early morning, and the Jews did not enter the Praetorium, to avoid being defiled and unable to eat the Passover. They would not cross the threshold for fear of ritual defilement on the morning they delivered an innocent man to be killed. So Pilate came out to them on the pavement and opened the trial: “What accusation are you bringing against this man?” Their answer was not an accusation at all: “If He were not a criminal,” they replied, “we would not have handed Him over to you.” Pilate called the bluff: “You take Him and judge Him by your own law,” Pilate told them. “We are not permitted to execute anyone,” the Jews replied. There it was, in the open, in the first exchange. The verdict had been reached before the charge; all they needed from Rome was the method of execution, and John notes that this fulfilled the word Jesus had spoken about the kind of death he would die: not stoning, but lifting up.

Pilate went back inside, summoned Jesus, and asked the political question: “Are You the King of the Jews?” Jesus turned the interview around at once: “Are you saying this on your own,” Jesus asked, “or did others tell you about Me?” “Am I a Jew?” Pilate replied. “Your own people and chief priests handed You over to me. What have You done?” Then Jesus defined his kingship in the terms this Gospel has used since the temple courts: “My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight to prevent My arrest by the Jews. But now My kingdom is not of this realm.” No legions, no swords in gardens; Peter's one attempt had been ordered back into its sheath. “Then You are a king!” Pilate said. “You say that I am a king,” Jesus answered. “For this reason I was born and have come into the world, to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to My voice.”

“What is truth?” Pilate asked. And having said this, John writes, he went out again to the Jews. The most famous question of the trial is not answered, because the man who asked it did not stay for an answer. Outside, Pilate delivered his verdict, which never changed: “I find no basis for a charge against Him.” Then he offered the Passover custom, one prisoner released, and framed the choice with the title still on the table: “So then, do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?” “Not this man,” they shouted, “but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was an insurrectionist. The city chose a rebel who took up arms against Rome over a king whose servants were forbidden to fight.

So Pilate took Jesus and had him flogged, and the soldiers dressed the verdict in a costume: a crown of thorns, a purple robe, and again and again the greeting with slaps: “Hail, King of the Jews!” Once again Pilate came out and said, “Look, I am bringing Him out to you to let you know that I find no basis for a charge against Him.” When Jesus came out wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe, Pilate said to them, “Here is the man!” As soon as the chief priests and officers saw him, they shouted, “Crucify Him! Crucify Him!” “You take Him and crucify Him,” Pilate replied, “for I find no basis for a charge against Him.” Then the Jews finally produced the real charge, the one from the temple courts: “We have a law,” answered the Jews, “and according to that law He must die, because He declared Himself to be the Son of God.”

When Pilate heard that, he was even more afraid, and he went back in and asked the question under all the questions: “Where are You from?” he asked. But Jesus gave no answer. The man who had answered everything all Gospel long met this one with silence. Pilate threatened him with the machinery of empire: “Do You refuse to speak to me? Do You not know that I have authority to release You and authority to crucify You?” Jesus answered with the trial's true map of power: “You would have no authority over Me if it were not given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed Me over to you is guilty of greater sin.” From then on Pilate tried to release him. But the Jews found the pressure point of every Roman career and pressed it: “If you release this man, you are no friend of Caesar. Anyone who declares himself a king is defying Caesar.”

When Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement, Gabbatha, on the day of Preparation for the Passover, about the sixth hour, and made his last appeal to irony: “Here is your King!” At this, they shouted, “Away with Him! Away with Him! Crucify Him!” “Shall I crucify your King?” Pilate asked. “We have no king but Caesar,” replied the chief priests. The men who would not enter the Praetorium for fear of defilement renounced, in one sentence, the kingship of God their whole history was built on, and claimed Caesar instead. Then Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified, and the soldiers took him away.

title: It Is Finished
subtitle: John 19:17–42
description: Jesus carries his own cross, provides for his mother, finishes the work, and is buried by Joseph and Nicodemus in a garden tomb.
paragraphs: Carrying his own cross, he went out to the Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha. John has no Simon of Cyrene; in this Gospel no one carries the cross for him, the way no one in the garden had to be asked twice who he was. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on each side, with Jesus in the middle. Pilate had a notice posted on the cross, the charge sheet of the execution, and it read: JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS. Many of the Jews read the sign, because the place was near the city, and it was written in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek, the languages of religion, empire, and the street, so that the whole world could read Rome's verdict on the kingship. The chief priests protested the wording: “Do not write, ‘The King of the Jews,’ but only that He said, ‘I am the King of the Jews.’” Pilate answered, “What I have written, I have written.” The governor who could not hold his verdict held his sign.

Below the cross, the soldiers divided his garments into four parts, one for each soldier, with the tunic remaining. It was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, “Let us not tear it. Instead, let us cast lots to see who will get it.” This was to fulfill the Scripture: “They divided My garments among them, and cast lots for My clothing.” So that is what the soldiers did, gambling at the foot of the cross for a dead man's coat, unaware they were acting out a psalm.

Near the cross of Jesus stood his mother and her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene. The women stayed. And when Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he made a family out of the two of them from the cross: He said to His mother, “Woman, here is your son.” Then He said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” So from that hour, this disciple took her into his home. It is the one piece of earthly business John's Jesus transacts on the cross, a son provided for a mother, in a Gospel where the Son had no home of his own to leave her.

After this, knowing that everything had now been accomplished, and to fulfill the Scripture, Jesus said, “I am thirsty.” A jar of sour wine was sitting there, and they soaked a sponge in the wine, put it on a stalk of hyssop, the plant of the first Passover's doorposts, and lifted it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, He said, “It is finished.” And bowing His head, He yielded up His spirit. Not taken, not lost: yielded, by the shepherd who had said no one takes his life from him. There is no cry of forsakenness in John's account. The last word from the cross in this Gospel is a word of completion.

Because it was the day of Preparation, and the next day was a high Sabbath, the Jews asked Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken and the bodies removed. The soldiers broke the legs of the two men beside him, but when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. Instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water flowed out. And here John steps into his own story with the claim his Gospel opened with, the eyewitness claim: “The one who saw it has testified to this, and his testimony is true. He knows that he is telling the truth, so that you also may believe.” These things happened, he says, so that Scripture would be fulfilled: “Not one of His bones will be broken.” “They will look on the One they have pierced.”

Afterward, Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate for the body, and Pilate gave permission. And Nicodemus came too, the man who had first come to Jesus at night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds, a royal weight of burial spice carried in the daylight. The two secret believers of John's Gospel, the night visitor and the hidden disciple, came out of hiding for a corpse when the public disciples had scattered. They took the body and wrapped it in linen cloths with the spices, according to the Jewish burial custom. Now there was a garden in the place where Jesus was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. And because it was the day of Preparation and the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus there, in a garden, where an arrest had begun the night before in another.

title: Peace Be with You
subtitle: John 20:1–31
description: Mary Magdalene finds the tomb empty, meets the risen Lord in the garden, and Thomas moves from conditions to the Gospel's highest confession.
paragraphs: Early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark, Mary Magdalene went to the tomb and saw that the stone had been removed from the entrance. She did not go in. She ran, to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, with the only explanation grief could assemble: “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb,” she said, “and we do not know where they have put Him!” Theft, desecration, a body stolen in the night. Nobody in this chapter starts the morning expecting a resurrection, least of all the woman who loved him most.

Then Peter and the other disciple set out for the tomb, and John records the footrace with the care of a man telling the truest thing he knows about himself: the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first. He bent down and looked in at the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Simon Peter arrived just after him and went straight in, and saw the linen cloths lying there, and the cloth that had been around Jesus' head rolled up, lying separate from the linen cloths. Grave robbers do not fold. Whatever had happened in that tomb, it had happened at leisure, in order. Then the other disciple also went in. “And he saw and believed.” Believed what, John does not say exactly, for they still did not understand from the Scripture that Jesus had to rise from the dead. He saw the emptiness arranged like evidence and believed ahead of his theology. Then the disciples returned to their homes. They left Mary there.

But Mary stood outside the tomb weeping, and as she wept, she bent down to look into the tomb, and she saw two angels in white sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and the other at the feet. “Woman, why are you weeping?” they asked. “Because they have taken my Lord away,” she said, “and I do not know where they have put Him.” When she had said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing there, but she did not recognize that it was Jesus. The risen Lord's first appearance in this Gospel is to a woman who mistakes him for the gardener, and he plays along with the two questions of the morning: “Woman, why are you weeping?” Jesus asked. “Whom are you seeking?” Thinking He was the gardener, she said, “Sir, if you have carried Him off, tell me where you have put Him, and I will get Him.” She offered to carry the body herself, alone, in the dark. Love was still trying to manage a corpse.

Jesus said to her, “Mary.” One word, her name, in the voice the sheep know. She turned and said to him in Hebrew, “Rabboni!” which means Teacher. “Do not cling to Me,” Jesus said, “for I have not yet ascended to the Father. But go and tell My brothers, ‘I am ascending to My Father and your Father, to My God and your God.’” My brothers. The men who had scattered and denied were brothers again in the first message of the resurrection, carried by the woman at the tomb: Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord!” The first preacher of the risen Christ in John's Gospel is the woman who came to manage a grave.

That evening, the first day of the week, the disciples were together with the doors locked for fear of the Jews, and Jesus came and stood among them, through the locks, and his first word to the men who abandoned him was the ordinary greeting made new: “Peace be with you!” He showed them his hands and his side, and the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord. Again Jesus said to them, “Peace be with you. As the Father has sent Me, so also I am sending you.” When He had said this, He breathed on them and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive anyone his sins, they are forgiven; if you withhold forgiveness from anyone, it is withheld.” The breath of God over the new creation, in a locked room, on the night of the first day.

Now Thomas called Didymus, one of the Twelve, was not with the disciples when Jesus came. So the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord!” But he replied with the terms that have named him ever since: “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.” Eight days later the disciples were inside again with the doors locked, and Thomas was with them, and Jesus came and stood among them and said, “Peace be with you.” Then he offered the absent man exactly the evidence he had demanded, without scolding him for the demand: “Put your finger here and look at My hands. Reach out your hand and put it into My side. Stop doubting and believe.” Thomas replied with the highest confession in the Gospel, from the man who had required the most proof: “My Lord and my God!” Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen Me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed.”

And the book closes its own cover with its purpose stated at last, the sentence every episode of it was written to serve: “Jesus performed many other signs in the presence of His disciples, which are not written in this book. But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name.” It sounds like an ending. John has one more chapter in him.

title: Breakfast by the Sea
subtitle: John 21:1–25
description: By the Sea of Tiberias the risen Jesus cooks breakfast, restores Peter beside a charcoal fire, and the Gospel signs its name.
paragraphs: Later, by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus again revealed himself to the disciples, and John tells it from the beginning, as if the book had one more morning in it. Simon Peter, Thomas called Didymus, Nathanael from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others were together, back in Galilee as they had been told, and Peter announced the plan of a man who has always solved uncertainty with work: “I am going fishing.” “We will go with you,” they said. So they went out and got into the boat, and fished their home water all night with all their old skill, “but caught nothing that night.” The empty net is where this Gospel's first disciples were found, years before, on this same sea. It is where they are found again.

Early in the morning, Jesus stood on the shore, but the disciples did not recognize that it was Jesus. He called out to them across the water the way a man on a dock calls to a boat coming in empty: “Children, do you have any fish?” “No,” they answered. He told them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it there, on a stranger's word, on the side of the boat they had not tried, “and they were unable to haul it in because of the great number of fish.” Then the disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter, “It is the Lord!” The beloved disciple recognized him from the pattern, the same way he had believed at the empty tomb by seeing how things were arranged. As soon as Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he had removed it to work, and jumped into the sea, swimming for shore while the others brought the boat and the net in behind him, a hundred yards of water between Peter and his shame.

When they landed, they saw a charcoal fire there with fish on it, and some bread. John's Gospel has two charcoal fires: one in the high priest's courtyard, where Peter warmed himself and denied, and one on this beach, laid by the risen Lord, with breakfast already cooking. Jesus told them, “Bring some of the fish you have just caught.” So Simon Peter went aboard and dragged the net ashore. “It was full of large fish, 153, but even with so many, the net was not torn.” John counts them, the way he counted the hour of his first following and the pounds of Nicodemus's spices; evidence has numbers in this Gospel. “Come, have breakfast,” Jesus said to them. None of the disciples dared to ask him who he was. They knew it was the Lord. Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and he did the same with the fish, host again at his own table, as at the hillside feeding and the upper room. “This was now the third time that Jesus appeared to the disciples after He was raised from the dead.”

When they had finished eating, Jesus asked Simon Peter, “Simon son of John, do you love Me more than these?” Not Peter, the rock name Jesus himself had given him in chapter one, but Simon son of John, the name he was born with. “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I love You.” Jesus replied, “Feed My lambs.” A second time: “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” “Yes, Lord,” he answered, “You know I love You.” Jesus told him, “Shepherd My sheep.” A third time: “Simon son of John, do you love Me?” Peter was deeply hurt that Jesus had asked him a third time, “Do you love Me?” Three questions beside a charcoal fire, for three denials beside the other one. “Lord, You know all things,” he replied. “You know I love You.” Jesus said to him, “Feed My sheep.” The restoration of Peter is not an apology scene. It is a commissioning, three answers deep, ending in a job: the sheep are the Lord's, and the man who denied him is to feed them.

Then Jesus told him the shape of his faithfulness: “Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were young, you dressed yourself and walked where you wanted; but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go.” Jesus said this, John explains, to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. And after he had said this, he told him the first command of the Gospel over again: Follow me. Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following them, the one who had leaned back against Jesus at the supper, and asked, “Lord, what about him?” Jesus answered, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you? You follow Me!” Peter's road was Peter's. The other man's road was not his business.

Because of this, the rumor spread among the brothers that this disciple would not die, and John corrects the rumor himself in the book's last movement, carefully, as he has corrected nothing else: Jesus did not say he would not die, but only, “If I want him to remain until I return, what is that to you?” Then the Gospel puts down its pen with the witness's signature: “This is the disciple who testifies to these things and who has written them down. And we know that his testimony is true.” And there are many more things that Jesus did: “There are many more things that Jesus did. If all of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have space for the books that would be written.” The book that began with the Word who was with God in the beginning ends with the confession that the world is too small a shelf for him.
